Summary: On March 14, the checkout service was unavailable for 42 minutes. During this time, about 3,200 customers were unable to complete their purchases.

Timeline: At 14:05, a new version of the payment service was deployed. At 14:12, monitoring alerts showed a sharp increase in error rates. The on-call engineer started investigating at 14:15. At 14:40, the team decided to roll back the deployment, and the service fully recovered at 14:47.

Root cause: The new version introduced a connection leak. Database connections were opened but never closed, so the connection pool was exhausted after a few minutes of normal traffic.

What went well: Alerts were triggered quickly, and the rollback process worked as expected.

What went wrong: The issue was not detected in staging because staging traffic is much lower than production traffic. It also took 25 minutes to decide to roll back.

Action items: add load tests to the deployment pipeline; create a rule to roll back automatically if error rates exceed 5%; add a check for unclosed connections in code reviews.

quick-cache is a lightweight in-memory cache for Node.js applications. It helps you reduce latency and database load by storing the results of expensive operations.

Installation: run npm install quick-cache. Node.js 18 or later is required.

Usage: create a cache with a default time-to-live, or TTL, in seconds. Call the get method with a key; if the value is not cached, provide a function that loads it. The result will be stored and returned on the next call until it expires.

Configuration: you can set a maximum number of entries. When the limit is reached, the least recently used items are removed first. Setting the TTL to zero disables expiration, which is not recommended for data that changes often.

Contributing: pull requests are welcome. Please open an issue first to discuss what you would like to change, and make sure to update the tests as appropriate. This project is licensed under the MIT License.

A good pull request makes life easier for everyone on the team. Reviewers understand your changes faster, bugs are caught earlier, and the project history becomes a useful source of documentation.

Keep it small. Large pull requests are hard to review, so they often receive superficial feedback. If a change touches many files, consider splitting it into several smaller pull requests that can be reviewed independently.

Write a clear description. Explain what the change does, why it is needed and how it was tested. Screenshots are extremely helpful for user interface changes. If there are parts you are unsure about, say so: it shows honesty and directs the reviewer's attention to where it matters most.

Respond to feedback professionally. Comments on your code are not comments on you. Thank reviewers for their time, ask questions when something isn't clear, and don't be afraid to explain your reasoning if you disagree. The goal is not to win the discussion but to ship better software together.

Sofía is twenty-seven years old. She lives in Medellín with her friend Daniel. Daniel is a chef, and he cooks amazing food. Sofía is a software developer, but she works for a small local company and she wants something new.

One Monday morning, she opens her laptop and sees an email from a company in London. The subject says: "Job offer". Sofía reads the email three times. She can't believe it. The company wants her to join their team as a remote developer.

"Daniel! Come here!" she shouts. Daniel runs from the kitchen with a spoon in his hand. "What happened? Are you OK?"

"I got the job! The job in London!"

"That's fantastic! But wait... do you have to move to London?"

"No, it's remote. I can work from here. But there's one problem," Sofía says. "All the meetings are in English. My English is... OK, but not great."

Daniel smiles. "Then you need to practise every day. You can start tonight. I'm making arepas, and you can tell me about the job. In English!"

It's Sofía's first day. The meeting starts at 9 a.m. in London, so it's 3 a.m. in Medellín... No, wait. Sofía checks again. London is five hours ahead, so the meeting is at 4 a.m. her time? No! The meeting is at 3 p.m. in London, so it's 9 a.m. in Medellín. Perfect.

She makes a big cup of coffee and turns on her camera. There are four people in the call. A man with grey hair says, "Hi everyone, I'm Mark. I'm the team lead. Welcome, Sofía!"

"Thank you. Nice to meet you," Sofía says. Her voice is a little nervous.

"This is Priya, our designer. She lives in Toronto. And this is Tom. He's a junior developer, like you were a few years ago."

Tom waves. "Hi Sofía! Don't worry, everybody is friendly here."

Mark speaks very fast. Sofía doesn't understand everything, but she writes the important words in a notebook: "sprint", "backlog", "deploy on Thursday". After the meeting, she sends a message to Tom: "Sorry, can you explain what a sprint is here? I want to be sure."

Tom answers in two minutes. "Sure! No problem. Asking questions is a good thing."

On Saturday, Sofía doesn't work. She goes with Daniel to the market early in the morning. Daniel wants to open a small restaurant, and he needs fresh fruit and vegetables for a new menu.

"Why do you want a restaurant?" Sofía asks. "You have a good job at the hotel."

"Yes, but I always cook what my boss wants. I want to cook my own food. Colombian food with a modern style."

At the market, a tourist from Canada asks Daniel about a strange fruit. "Excuse me, what is this?"

Daniel looks at Sofía. He doesn't speak much English. Sofía helps him. "It's called lulo. It's a little sour, but it's great for juice."

The tourist buys five lulos and says thank you. Daniel is surprised. "Your English is good, Sofía!"

"It's getting better. I practise every day now. Hey... maybe your restaurant needs a menu in English, too. Lots of tourists come to Medellín."

Daniel thinks about it. "OK. You help me with the English menu, and I cook dinner for you every Friday. Deal?"

"Deal!"

It was Friday afternoon, and Sofía was looking forward to a quiet weekend. She had finished her tasks, and Daniel was already cooking dinner. Then her phone buzzed. It was a message from Mark: "Urgent. Customers can't log in. Can you have a look?"

Sofía's heart started beating faster. The login page was part of the code she had changed that week. She opened the logs and saw hundreds of errors. While she was reading them, Tom joined the call.

"I think it's my fault," Tom said quietly. "I deployed a small change an hour ago. I didn't run all the tests."

Sofía didn't get angry. She remembered her first job, when she had deleted a whole database by mistake. "Don't worry. Let's find the problem together. Can you share your screen?"

After forty minutes, they found it. A configuration file had the wrong value. Tom fixed it, and Sofía checked everything twice. The customers could log in again.

Later, Mark wrote in the team chat: "Great job, both of you. Next week let's talk about how to stop this happening again. No blame, just better processes."

Sofía closed her laptop and went to the kitchen. "Sorry I'm late. The food smells amazing."

"It was hot an hour ago," Daniel laughed. "But it's still good."

Priya, the designer from Toronto, sent Sofía a private message one morning. "Do you have ten minutes? I've got an idea, but I'm not sure if it's crazy."

They started a video call. Priya explained that many users had complained about the app's checkout process. "It has six steps," she said. "If you ask me, it should have three. People get tired and leave before they pay."

Sofía agreed, but she could see a problem. "I see what you mean, but changing it will take a lot of time. Mark wants us to focus on the new features."

"That's exactly why I need your help," Priya said. "If we show him numbers, he'll listen. Can you find out how many people leave at each step?"

Sofía spent the afternoon working with the data. The result surprised both of them: almost forty percent of users left at step four, where they had to create an account.

The next day they presented the numbers to Mark. He was quiet for a moment. Then he said, "OK. I wasn't expecting that. Let's try a guest checkout without an account. Priya, can you design it? Sofía, can you build it in the next sprint?"

After the meeting, Priya sent a message with three coffee emojis. Sofía answered: "Your crazy idea wasn't so crazy after all."

Daniel had finally found a place for his restaurant, a small house with a garden near Parque Lleras. The owner lived in Miami and only spoke English, so Daniel asked Sofía to help him with the phone call.

"I'm so nervous," he said. "What if he asks me something I don't understand?"

"Then I'll translate. But try to say the first part yourself. We practised it."

The owner, Mr. Harris, answered after three rings. Daniel took a deep breath. "Good morning, Mr. Harris. My name is Daniel Restrepo. I'm calling about the house on Calle 10. I'd like to rent it for a restaurant."

Sofía gave him a thumbs up. Mr. Harris asked several questions: how long Daniel wanted to rent it for, whether he would make changes to the kitchen, and when he could start. Sofía helped with the difficult parts, but Daniel understood more than he expected.

Then Mr. Harris said something that made them both stop. "The rent is two thousand dollars a month, and I need six months in advance."

Daniel looked at Sofía. It was much more than he had. Sofía whispered, "Ask him if it's negotiable."

"Is the price... negotiable?" Daniel asked.

There was a long silence. "Well," Mr. Harris said, "if you can sign a contract for two years, I could accept three months in advance."

When they hung up, Daniel was smiling. "I can't believe I negotiated in English!"

Six months after joining the company, Sofía received an unexpected invitation to a one-to-one meeting with Mark. She spent the morning wondering whether she had done something wrong.

"I'll get straight to the point," Mark said. "We're setting up a new team to rebuild the payments system, and I'd like you to lead it."

Sofía was speechless. Leading a team meant running meetings, giving feedback and, above all, speaking English all day long, often under pressure. "I'm flattered," she managed to say. "Having said that, I'm not sure I'm ready. My English still lets me down sometimes, especially when people speak fast."

Mark nodded. "I appreciate your honesty. But when it comes to communication, what matters most is being clear, not sounding like a native speaker. You ask good questions, you explain things simply and you never pretend to understand when you don't. Those are rare skills."

Sofía asked for a couple of days to think it over. That evening she talked to Daniel, who was exhausted after a long day at the restaurant, which had opened the month before.

"Do you remember the phone call with Mr. Harris?" he said. "I was terrified, and you told me to say the first part myself. Maybe you should take your own advice."

The following Monday, Sofía accepted the offer, on one condition: that the company paid for a public speaking course. Mark agreed immediately.
to get straight to the point

Leading a team turned out to be harder than Sofía had anticipated, and not because of the technical challenges. Tom, who had joined her team, had been missing deadlines for weeks. His code was good when it arrived, but it rarely arrived on time, and the rest of the team had started to notice.

Sofía kept putting off the conversation. She liked Tom; he had been the first person to make her feel welcome. But at the end of the day, it was her responsibility.

She prepared carefully, using a structure from her public speaking course: describe the situation, explain the impact, and ask questions before drawing conclusions.

"Tom, can I share something I've noticed? The last three tasks were delivered between four and six days late. That's had an impact on Priya, who couldn't start her designs, and on our release date. I'm not here to blame you. I'd really like to understand what's going on."

There was a long pause. Then Tom admitted that his mother had been ill and that he had been travelling to Leeds every weekend to look after her. He hadn't said anything because he was afraid it would sound like an excuse.

"It doesn't sound like an excuse at all," Sofía said. "It sounds like something we should have known about. Let's look at your workload and see what we can move. And please, next time, tell me earlier. I'd much rather adjust a plan than lose a teammate."

Tom looked relieved. A month later, he was meeting every deadline, and he had become the team's most reliable reviewer.

Daniel's restaurant had been open for almost a year when a food critic from an international travel magazine booked a table without warning. Daniel only found out because the critic's assistant called to confirm the reservation and accidentally mentioned the magazine's name.

Panic spread through the kitchen. Daniel asked Sofía to come and help at the front of the restaurant, since she was the only person he trusted who could chat comfortably in English.

The critic turned out to be a soft-spoken woman called Helen, who asked detailed questions about every dish. Sofía explained that the menu was inspired by Daniel's grandmother's recipes, reinterpreted with modern techniques. When Helen asked why the dessert combined lulo with dark chocolate, Sofía realised she didn't know the answer, so she did what she had learned at work: instead of making something up, she said, "That's a great question. Let me ask the chef."

Daniel came out of the kitchen, wiping his hands on his apron, and answered in slow but confident English. "The lulo is sour, the chocolate is bitter. Together, they are like Medellín: a little intense, but you want more."

Helen laughed and wrote something in her notebook.

Two months later the article was published. The headline read: "A taste of Medellín, one honest answer at a time." Daniel framed it and hung it next to the kitchen door.

When the organisers of a developer conference in Lisbon invited Sofía to give a talk on how her team had rebuilt the payments system, her first instinct was to decline. Speaking to a room of three hundred engineers, many of them native speakers, struck her as an entirely different proposition from running a stand-up meeting.

What changed her mind was a remark Priya made over a video call. "You keep assuming the audience wants a flawless accent. What they actually want is someone who's been through the mess and can tell them what went wrong. Nobody else can tell that story."

Sofía spent weeks preparing. Rather than memorising a script, she rehearsed the key transitions until she could deliver them in her sleep, and she deliberately left room for improvisation. She also recorded herself and noticed she tended to rush whenever she felt insecure, so she wrote a single word at the top of each slide note: "Breathe."

On the day, ten minutes into the talk, the projector died. For a few seconds the room was silent. Sofía felt the familiar panic rising, then heard herself say, "Well, I did promise you a talk about systems failing in production." The audience burst out laughing, and by the time a technician had fixed the projector, she had already explained the architecture by drawing it on a whiteboard.

Afterwards, a senior engineer from a major bank approached her. "I've been to dozens of these conferences," he said, "and that was the first time I actually understood how a payments migration works." On the flight back, Sofía caught herself thinking, for the first time, not in Spanish or in English, but simply in ideas.

The conference talk had consequences Sofía hadn't foreseen. Within a fortnight she had received two job offers. The first came from the bank whose engineer had approached her in Lisbon: a senior architect role in London, with a salary nearly double her current one and a relocation package thrown in. The second, less glamorous but intriguing, came from a small start-up in Medellín that was building software for local farmers to sell directly to restaurants.

On paper, the decision was straightforward. In practice, it was anything but. Moving to London would mean leaving Daniel, whose restaurant was finally thriving, and starting from scratch in a city where she knew no one. On the other hand, it was the kind of opportunity that had seemed unthinkable two years earlier, when she had read that first email three times in disbelief.

She drew up a list of pros and cons, which, predictably, solved nothing. So she turned to the people whose judgement she trusted most. Mark, to her surprise, urged her to consider the start-up seriously. "Big companies will always be there," he said. "Chances to build something from the ground up, with people you care about, are far rarer." Priya took the opposite view: "You've earned the right to be ambitious. Don't talk yourself out of it."

Daniel, characteristically, said very little and cooked her favourite meal. Only at the end of the evening did he add: "Whatever you choose, make sure it's because you want it, not because you're afraid of the alternative."

Sofía went to bed that night realising that, for the first time, the language she would work in was no longer the deciding factor. The decision had become, quite simply, a question of who she wanted to be.
to talk yourself out of something

A year later, on a Monday morning not unlike the one on which she had first opened that email from London, Sofía was sitting in a cramped office above a bakery in Envigado, interviewing candidates for the start-up she had chosen to join as its chief technology officer.

The last candidate of the day was a twenty-three-year-old developer called Valentina, whose technical test had been outstanding. Midway through the interview, Sofía switched to English, as the company now worked with clients in Canada and the United States. Valentina's confidence visibly evaporated. She stumbled over her words, apologised twice, and finally admitted, in Spanish, that her English was "more or less A2".

Sofía put down her pen. "Can I tell you something? Four years ago, I was exactly where you are now. I used to write down every word I didn't understand in meetings and look them up at night. I recorded myself, I made a fool of myself on phone calls, and I once told a whole meeting I was 'constipated' when I meant I had a cold."

Valentina laughed in spite of herself.

"Your English will improve if you use it every single day, even when it's uncomfortable. Especially when it's uncomfortable. The code you wrote, on the other hand, is something I can't teach. We'd like to offer you the job."

That evening, Sofía walked to Daniel's restaurant, where Mark and Priya, visiting Colombia for the first time, were waiting at a table in the garden. Tom had joined them by video, the laptop propped against a bottle of wine. Daniel came out with a dessert that wasn't on the menu: lulo and dark chocolate.

"To Code & Coffee," Priya said, raising her glass.

"And to asking questions," Tom added from the screen.

Sofía raised hers and said nothing for a moment. Then, in an English that was no longer something she performed but simply the way she spoke, she said, "To the first email. And to everyone who made me answer it."

Last January I decided to try an experiment: one month without social media. I deleted Instagram, TikTok and Facebook from my phone. I kept WhatsApp, because I need it for work.

The first week was really hard. I kept picking up my phone without thinking, and I felt anxious because I didn't know what my friends were doing. I realised that I used to check my phone more than a hundred times a day.

By the second week, things started to change. I was sleeping better, because I wasn't looking at a screen in bed. I read two books, something I hadn't done for years, and I started cooking more.

The biggest surprise was my relationships. Instead of liking my friends' photos, I called them or met them for coffee. Our conversations were longer and more real.

When the month finished, I installed Instagram again, but I use it differently now. I've turned off notifications and I only check it once a day. I don't think social media is bad, but I've learnt that I need to control it, not the other way round.

Two months ago, I ordered a new laptop online. The website promised delivery in three days, but after two weeks it still hadn't arrived. I called customer service four times. Each time, a different person told me that the laptop was "on its way".

I was getting really frustrated, so I decided to write a formal complaint. A friend who works in sales gave me some advice: be polite, be clear and say exactly what you want.

In my email, I explained the situation with dates and order numbers. I said that I was disappointed with the service and that I wanted either the laptop within five days or a full refund. I didn't shout or insult anyone.

The next day, the manager called me personally. She apologised, explained that there had been a problem with the warehouse, and offered me the laptop the same week plus a 20% discount on my next order.

The lesson? Anger doesn't solve problems, but a calm, organised complaint often does.

When Daniel moved from Cali to Toronto to study, he thought the hardest thing would be the language. He had studied English for years and he could understand films without subtitles, so he felt confident.

In reality, the language was only one part of the challenge. People spoke much faster than in the films, and they used lots of expressions he had never heard. But the biggest surprise was the weather. His first winter was minus twenty degrees, and he didn't even have proper boots.

He also missed the food and the warmth of people back home. "In Colombia, you talk to strangers all the time. Here, people are friendly but more reserved," he says.

After a year, though, Daniel feels at home. He has made friends from all over the world, he has learnt to love ice skating and his English has improved enormously. "If I had to give advice to someone moving abroad," he says, "I'd tell them to be patient. The first six months are difficult for everyone."

In recent years, hundreds of companies around the world have tested a four-day working week. The idea is simple: employees work 80% of the time, keep 100% of their salary, and promise to maintain at least 100% of their productivity.

The results of the largest trials have been surprisingly positive. Most participating companies reported that productivity stayed the same or even improved, while staff reported lower levels of stress and burnout. Many employees said they used the extra day for exercise, family or simply resting, which made them more focused when they returned to work. As a result, the majority of companies decided to keep the new schedule after the trial ended.

However, critics point out that the model doesn't work for every sector. Hospitals, schools and restaurants, for example, need people present every day, so reducing hours often means hiring more staff, which increases costs. Others argue that some employees simply squeeze five days of work into four, ending up with longer and more intense days.

The debate is far from over. What seems clear is that the traditional nine-to-five, five-day week, designed more than a century ago, is no longer the only option.

Why is it so hard to start going to the gym, yet so easy to keep checking our phones? According to researchers, the answer lies in how habits are formed.

A habit, they explain, is a loop with three parts: a cue, a routine and a reward. The cue is a trigger, such as feeling bored or hearing a notification. The routine is the behaviour itself, like opening social media. The reward is the pleasant feeling we get, which teaches the brain to repeat the loop next time.

The problem with "good" habits is that their rewards are often delayed. The benefits of exercise or studying a language appear weeks or months later, whereas the reward of checking your phone is instant. That's why experts recommend creating small, immediate rewards for good behaviour, such as tracking your progress or enjoying a favourite coffee after a workout.

Another effective strategy is "habit stacking": attaching a new habit to an existing one. For instance, "After I make my morning coffee, I will review ten English words." By linking the new behaviour to a cue that already exists, it becomes much easier to remember and repeat.

Finally, researchers insist that consistency matters more than intensity. Studying for ten minutes every day is likely to produce better results than studying for three hours once a week.

Every year, millions of people travel to the same famous destinations: Venice, Barcelona, Machu Picchu, Cartagena. Tourism brings money and jobs, but in many places it has become a victim of its own success.

In some historic centres, rents have risen so much that local residents can no longer afford to live there. Apartments have been turned into short-term holiday rentals, and traditional shops have been replaced by souvenir stores. The result is a neighbourhood that looks beautiful in photos but has lost its soul.

Natural sites suffer too. Popular trails are damaged by thousands of visitors, and fragile ecosystems are polluted by waste. Some destinations have responded by limiting the number of daily visitors or introducing tourist taxes, measures that were unthinkable a decade ago.

I'm not suggesting we should stop travelling. Travel opens our minds and supports local economies. But we could all travel more responsibly: visiting less crowded places, staying longer instead of rushing between cities, and spending money in businesses owned by local people. If we don't change the way we travel, the places we love may not survive in the form we know them.

Conventional wisdom holds that more choice is always better. If one type of jam makes customers happy, surely twenty-four types will make them happier still. Yet a growing body of research suggests that, beyond a certain point, an abundance of options can be counterproductive.

In a frequently cited experiment, shoppers who were presented with a display of twenty-four varieties of jam were considerably more likely to stop and look than those who saw only six. However, they were roughly ten times less likely to actually make a purchase. Faced with too many alternatives, people seemed to become paralysed, unable to commit to a decision for fear of choosing wrongly.

The phenomenon extends well beyond supermarkets. Psychologists argue that excessive choice in careers, relationships and even streaming platforms can lead to anxiety, regret and a nagging sense that we might have done better. Paradoxically, those who insist on finding the "best" option, so-called maximisers, tend to report lower levels of satisfaction than "satisficers", who settle for an option that is simply good enough.

That said, the evidence is not entirely conclusive. Subsequent studies have struggled to replicate the original findings consistently, and some researchers contend that the effect depends heavily on context, such as how familiar people are with the product or how options are organised. What seems undeniable, however, is that more is not invariably better, and that learning when to stop searching may be a skill worth cultivating.

Most of us assume that our memories function rather like a video recording: an accurate, if occasionally blurry, record of what happened. Decades of research in cognitive psychology, however, paint a very different picture. Memory, it turns out, is not so much retrieved as reconstructed every time we recall an event.

In a series of landmark studies, participants watched footage of a car accident and were then asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed into" or "hit" each other. Those who heard the word "smashed" not only estimated higher speeds but, a week later, were far more likely to falsely remember seeing broken glass at the scene. A single word had been enough to alter their recollection.

The implications are profound, particularly for the justice system. Eyewitness testimony has long been regarded as among the most persuasive forms of evidence in court, yet it has been implicated in a substantial proportion of wrongful convictions later overturned by DNA evidence. Witnesses are rarely lying; rather, they are sincerely convinced of memories that have been shaped by leading questions, conversations with others or media coverage.

None of this means that memory is useless. For everyday purposes, it serves us remarkably well. But it should make us more humble about the certainty with which we recount the past, and more cautious about treating confident recollection as proof of accuracy.

The aim of this report is to examine the reasons behind the high staff turnover recorded in the customer service department over the past year and to propose measures to address the issue.

Findings
Exit interviews conducted with 34 former employees reveal three recurring concerns. Firstly, over two thirds of respondents cited a lack of opportunities for career progression as their primary reason for leaving. Secondly, many felt that their workload had increased substantially without a corresponding rise in salary. Finally, a significant number reported that they had received little or no feedback from their managers, which left them feeling undervalued.

Recommendations
In light of these findings, it is recommended that the company introduce a clear career framework, outlining the skills and experience required for promotion at each level. Furthermore, workloads should be reviewed on a quarterly basis to ensure they remain manageable. It would also be advisable to provide training for managers in giving regular, constructive feedback.

Conclusion
While implementing these measures will require an initial investment, the cost of recruiting and training new staff is considerably higher. Should the proposals be adopted, turnover is likely to fall significantly within twelve months.

There is a seductive logic to measurement. What gets measured, the adage goes, gets managed, and in an era awash with data, it has become almost an article of faith that any institution worth its salt should quantify its performance. Hospitals are ranked by waiting times, schools by examination results, academics by citation counts.

Yet the relentless pursuit of metrics carries a hidden cost, one that the economist Charles Goodhart identified decades ago. When a measure becomes a target, he observed, it ceases to be a good measure. Surgeons judged on mortality rates may quietly decline to operate on high-risk patients; teachers evaluated on test scores may "teach to the test" at the expense of genuine understanding; police forces rewarded for falling crime figures may be tempted to reclassify offences. In each case, the number improves while the underlying reality it was meant to capture stays the same, or even deteriorates.

None of this is to suggest that measurement is inherently pernicious. Data can expose inefficiencies, reveal inequalities and hold the powerful to account. The problem arises when numbers are mistaken for the things they represent, when the map is confused with the territory. Many of the qualities we value most, such as trust, curiosity and professional judgement, are precisely those that resist quantification.

The challenge, then, is not to abandon metrics but to use them with humility: as instruments for inquiry rather than instruments of control. That requires something no spreadsheet can supply, namely the willingness to accept that not everything that counts can be counted.

Language learning apps promise fluency in weeks, and social media is replete with polyglots who claim to have mastered Mandarin in a summer. It is hardly surprising, then, that so many learners feel disheartened when, after years of study, they still stumble over phrasal verbs or fail to catch a joke at a dinner party.

The disconnect stems, in part, from a misunderstanding of what advanced proficiency entails. Reaching an intermediate level is largely a matter of acquiring grammar and core vocabulary, which can indeed be achieved relatively quickly with sustained effort. Beyond that point, however, progress becomes less visible. The gap between a competent speaker and a truly proficient one lies in thousands of collocations, idioms, cultural references and subtle shifts of register, knowledge that is absorbed gradually through extensive exposure rather than memorised in lists.

This is why the so-called intermediate plateau is so common, and so dispiriting. Learners continue to put in the hours yet feel they are standing still. In reality, they are consolidating: their comprehension is deepening, their recall becoming faster, their intuition for what sounds natural growing sharper. These changes are real, but they rarely announce themselves.

The remedy, if there is one, is to shift from studying the language to living in it: reading novels rather than graded texts, listening to podcasts at native speed, writing for real audiences. Above all, it means accepting that mastery is less a destination than a direction, a process measured not in weeks but in years.

In recent years, working from home has become increasingly common, especially since the pandemic.
While it offers clear benefits, it also presents some challenges.
One of the main advantages is flexibility.
Employees save time and money on commuting, and they can organise their day around their personal needs.
Furthermore, many companies have found that productivity does not decrease when staff work remotely, and they can even reduce the cost of office space.
However, it could be argued that remote work has a negative impact on teamwork and learning.
Junior employees, in particular, may find it difficult to develop their skills without regular contact with experienced colleagues.
In addition, some workers feel isolated and find it hard to separate their professional and private lives.
Taking everything into account, I believe that a hybrid model is the most effective solution.
If employees spent two or three days in the office, they would benefit from both the flexibility of remote work and the human connection of the workplace.

Few technologies have advanced as rapidly as artificial intelligence, and few have generated such intense debate.
While some believe that strict regulation is essential to protect society, others warn that it could stifle innovation.
This essay will argue that regulation is necessary, provided that it is targeted rather than restrictive.
Proponents of minimal regulation contend that excessive rules would slow progress and push companies to relocate to countries with looser legislation.
There is some merit in this view: poorly designed laws could indeed place smaller firms at a disadvantage, since only large corporations can afford complex compliance processes.
Nevertheless, it would be naive to assume that the market will regulate itself.
AI systems are already being used to make decisions about loans, job applications and even medical treatment, often with little transparency.
Should these systems contain hidden biases, the consequences for marginalised groups could be severe.
What is more, the potential for misinformation and fraud is growing at an alarming rate.
The solution, therefore, lies not in banning technologies but in regulating their use according to risk.
Applications that affect people's rights or safety ought to be subject to independent audits and clear accountability, whereas low-risk tools could remain largely unrestricted.
On balance, I would argue that well-designed regulation is not an obstacle to innovation but a precondition for public trust.
Without that trust, AI is unlikely to reach its full potential.
The aim of this report is to assess the effectiveness of the current onboarding process for new employees and to recommend improvements.
A survey of 25 employees who joined in the last year indicates that the onboarding process is perceived as disorganised.
Over half reported that they did not receive the necessary equipment on their first day, and many stated that they had to rely on colleagues to understand basic procedures.
Furthermore, it was found that new employees take on average four months to become fully productive, compared to the industry benchmark of two.

In light of these findings, it is recommended that a structured two-week onboarding programme be introduced, including a clear schedule, training sessions and a designated mentor for each new employee.
It would also be advisable to prepare all equipment and system access before the start date.
Finally, a short feedback survey should be conducted after the first month in order to identify further areas for improvement.
While these measures will require some time and coordination, they are relatively inexpensive.
Should they be adopted, new employees are likely to become productive considerably sooner, which would benefit both the teams and the company as a whole.

There is no denying that social media has transformed the way we relate to one another.
It allows us to stay in touch with relatives abroad, find communities of like-minded people and share our lives instantly.
For many, particularly those who feel isolated, these platforms have been a lifeline.
What is rarely discussed, however, is the quality of these connections.
Paradoxically, the more time we spend interacting online, the lonelier many of us seem to feel.
Likes and comments offer a quick sense of approval, but they are no substitute for the depth of a face-to-face conversation.
It is the effort of meeting in person, the awkward silences, the shared laughter, that builds genuine intimacy.
None of this means we should abandon our accounts.
Perhaps the real question is not whether social media is good or bad, but whether we use it to enrich our relationships or to replace them.
The next time you are tempted to scroll through a friend's photos, you might consider calling them instead.
Chances are, they would be glad to hear from you.
It has become something of a truism that technological progress has liberated humanity.
We can communicate instantly across continents, access the sum of human knowledge from our pockets and work from almost anywhere.
Yet this narrative of emancipation, compelling as it is, obscures a more ambivalent reality.
There is no denying that technology has expanded the range of choices available to us.

Remote work has freed millions from the tyranny of the daily commute; online education has opened doors to those who could never have afforded a university; social platforms have given a voice to communities long ignored by traditional media.
To dismiss these gains would be not only ungrateful but misguided.
This view, however, rests on the premise that more options necessarily translate into greater freedom.
In practice, the very devices that connect us also monitor us, harvesting data to predict and shape our behaviour.
The algorithms that curate our news feeds subtly narrow the range of opinions we encounter, while the expectation of constant availability has blurred the boundary between work and private life.
Herein lies the paradox: the tools that promise autonomy may, if left unchecked, erode it.
What matters, then, is not technology itself but the conditions under which it is designed and used.
Where users understand and control how their data is employed, and where regulation ensures transparency, technology can genuinely enhance freedom.
Where it is driven solely by the imperative to capture attention, it risks becoming a gilded cage.
Ultimately, the question is not whether technological progress makes us freer, but whether we are prepared to shape it so that it does.
Imagine, for a moment, a child who can recite the dates of every major battle in history but cannot tell a reliable news source from a fabricated one.
Imagine a graduate who has memorised hundreds of formulas yet has never been asked to solve a problem that matters to her community.
This, I would argue, is the paradox at the heart of many education systems today.
Let me be clear: knowledge matters.
But in a world where information is abundant and instantly available, what distinguishes an educated person is no longer how much they know, but what they can do with what they know.
Can they collaborate with people who think differently?
Can they adapt when the jobs of today disappear tomorrow?
The reform I am proposing is neither radical nor untested.

It rests on three pillars: teaching critical thinking explicitly, from primary school onwards; replacing a significant proportion of standardised exams with project-based assessment; and investing in the training of teachers, who remain, without doubt, the single most important factor in any classroom.
Countries that have embraced similar approaches have seen not only higher levels of student engagement but also stronger results in international assessments.
The evidence, in short, is on our side.
It is not enough to update our textbooks; we must rethink what we expect education to achieve.
The question before us is not whether we can afford to reform our schools, but whether we can afford not to.
